title: Multi-armed bandit laboratory
summary: Run the methods of Chapter 2 on an $n$-armed bandit and watch them learn: greedy and $\varepsilon$-greedy action selection, sample-average or constant-$\alpha$ estimates, optimistic initial values, UCB and the gradient bandit. Step through one run update by update with every number shown, then average many runs to see the curves of Figures 2.1–2.4.
guide: Step through greedy with sample averages. Notice that once one action's estimate is ahead it is chosen again and again: greedy selection never tries actions that look worse.
Switch to $\varepsilon = 0.1$. On each step the inspector shows whether the $\varepsilon$ branch was taken. Check the update $Q \leftarrow Q + \tfrac1N(R - Q)$ against the numbers shown.

Average 2000 runs of greedy, $\varepsilon = 0.01$ and $\varepsilon = 0.1$ (the Figure 2.1 preset). Greedy should level off near an average reward of 1 and find the optimal action in about a third of the runs.
Try the Figure 2.2 preset: optimistic greedy ($Q_1 = 5$, $\alpha = 0.1$) starts worse than realistic $\varepsilon$-greedy and overtakes it.
Try the Figure 2.3 preset and look at step 11 for UCB. It has just tried each of the 10 arms once and now picks the best-looking one.
Try the Figure 2.4 preset (true values centred on +4) with and without the baseline $\bar R_t$.

verification.note: 300 seeded runs reproduce the behaviour the draft reports; further checks cover Figures 2.2–2.4.

flags.note: Equation (2.9) is printed with an unmatched parenthesis in the numerator (see the equation's note). The lab computes the soft-max as $e^{H_t(a)} / \sum_b e^{H_t(b)}$.
